title: Why Houses Cost So Much in the UK

beats.say: In the late nineteen nineties, a typical home in England cost around four times a typical full time salary. Today, it's closer to eight times. In London, it's over ten. So what happened?
According to the Office for National Statistics, the median home in England cost about seven point six times median annual earnings in twenty twenty five. In London, it was about ten point six.

vis.label: times earnings for a typical home in England, 2025

beats.say: There's no single reason. It's a mix of things that have built up over decades. Let's go through the main ones.

vis.text: No single reason. A mix of many.

beats.say: Part one. Not enough homes.
The first reason most people point to is supply. For decades, Britain hasn't built as many homes as it needs. Meanwhile, the population has grown, people live longer, and more people live alone.
Governments have set targets, like three hundred thousand homes a year in England. Those targets have often been missed.

Why is building slow? Planning rules can be complex. Local opposition can block new developments. Land in popular areas is expensive. And housebuilders tend to build at a pace that protects their prices.

Britain also has lots of empty space between towns protected as green belt, to stop cities sprawling. Supporters say it protects the countryside. Critics say it limits building near where people want to live.
Part two. Cheap money.

The second big reason is the cost of borrowing. For most of the period from two thousand and nine to twenty twenty one, interest rates were extremely low. Cheap mortgages meant people could borrow more.
When people can borrow more, they can bid more for the same houses. If the number of homes doesn't rise much, prices go up. Cheaper borrowing gets built into higher prices.
This is why monthly payments can feel affordable even as prices soar. But it also means when interest rates rise, as they did from twenty twenty two, many buyers suddenly find they can borrow less.
Government schemes to help buyers, like Help to Buy, helped many people buy homes. But critics argued some of these schemes also helped push prices up, by boosting demand without enough new supply.

vis.text: Help to Buy: help, or higher prices?

beats.say: Part three. Houses as investments.

Homes in Britain have also become investments, not just places to live. Buy to let landlords grew in number, helped by special mortgages. Some homes were bought by investors from abroad. And many owners saw property as their retirement plan.

Those who already owned property often did very well, as prices rose. That wealth could then be passed down, helping their children buy. The result is a growing gap between those with family money and those without.

vis.title: Who's done well
items: Families who can help their kids

beats.say: Today, a large share of first time buyers get help from family to pay for a deposit. That's often called the bank of mum and dad.

vis.text: The bank of mum and dad.

beats.say: Part four. Wages fell behind.

At the same time, wages haven't kept pace. Over the long run, house prices in many areas grew much faster than earnings. The ratio of prices to earnings roughly doubled in England between the late nineties and the twenty twenties.

vis.title: House price to earnings ratio, England

beats.say: That's why saving for a deposit is so much harder now. A ten percent deposit on a typical home today is a much bigger share of a typical salary than it was for many of today's parents.

vis.text: The deposit is the biggest hurdle.

beats.say: Part five. The impact.
The effects are huge. Young people are buying later, or renting for longer. Rents have risen in many places. Some people stay in jobs or areas they'd rather leave, because moving is too expensive.
Higher housing costs also mean less money for everything else. When rent or a mortgage takes a big chunk of your pay, there's less left to save, spend or invest.
But it varies hugely by place. In ONS figures for twenty twenty five, some areas in the north of England were around four times earnings. Kensington and Chelsea in London was over twenty five times.
Part six. What might help?

There's no easy fix, and people disagree about the best approach. Ideas include building many more homes, reforming planning, building more social housing, changing taxes on property, and supporting first time buyers. Each has supporters and critics.
UK house prices aren't high because of one villain. They're the result of not enough building, cheap borrowing, homes becoming investments, and wages falling behind, all adding up over thirty years.

vis.text: Thirty years of causes, adding up.
